NHTSA announced today that they are proposing new rules aimed at removing U.S. federal regulatory barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as @Tesla's Cybercab.

The proposed changes include:
• Eliminating requirements for manually operated turn signal controls in vehicles without steering wheels or pedals: "NHTSA has concluded that the self-canceling and manually operated control requirements in the current standard are unnecessary for turn signal operating units that are installed on vehicles without manually operated driving controls."

• Allowing autonomous driving systems to control turn signals, hazard lights, and high/low beams without traditional driver-operated switches.

• Removing certain dashboard indicator requirements for turn signals and high beams in vehicles without manual driving controls.

• Allowing optional cyan-colored exterior lights to indicate when a vehicle is operating autonomously, with standardized requirements for their placement, brightness, and operation.

• Eliminating outdated restrictions on vertical headlight arrangements, giving automakers greater design flexibility.

• Allowing modern integrated headlights to be tested at manufacturer-specified voltages rather than requiring 12.8 volts.

NHTSA says the changes are intended to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, reduce costs, and enable innovation without compromising vehicle safety.

posts.text:
The best way to value high growth companies is using DCF (discounted cash flow) with multiple stages of growth rather than relative multiples or P/E relative to growth.  With DCF, one can estimate the free cash flow assuming t1 years of super growth, t2 years of transition growth,  and then perpetual or steady state growth.  Contrary to what many value investors will tell you, perpetual or steady state growth for a company can exceed the growth in nominal GDP if the company has permanent advantages (first movers’ technology, patents, distribution, brand) that aren’t likely to be arbitraged away as more competitors enter the market.  

Most important is to come up with an appropriate cost of equity to discount the equity free cash flows that reflects the riskiness of the stock, which can be higher or lower than the S&P 500 cost of equity. The reason DCFs are better than relative multiples as measurement tools is the latter tend to be arbitrary especially in a market such as today where multiples are high relative to history.

The road doesn’t care how tired you are.

I’ve spent decades living out of a suitcase. Different city, different time zone, same responsibility. 

Here’s what keeps me locked in:

1. I read my goals before bed and when I wake up. Hotel room or home, doesn’t matter.
2. I plan the trip around the meeting, not the other way around.
3. I sleep on the plane when I can. Rest is part of the work.
4. I drink water like it’s my job. Travel dehydrates you and it shows up in your decisions.
5. I move my body every day, even if it’s 15 minutes in the room.
6. I keep one habit from home so the day still feels like mine.
7. I prep the night before. No scrambling in the morning.
8. I talk to people. The Uber driver, the person next to me on the flight. Some of my best ideas came from strangers.
9. I call home. Staying connected keeps me grounded.
10. I remind myself why I got on the plane in the first place.

Motivation fades. Systems travel with you.

Send this to someone who’s heading out on a work trip soon ✈️

Pershing Square’s @BillAckman presents his proposed Fannie and Freddie privatization as a windfall for taxpayers. But assigning a higher market value to shares the government continues to hold does not, by itself, create new wealth for taxpayers.

Taxpayers already own valuable senior preferred-stock rights and warrants. Ackman wants Treasury’s preferred investment deemed repaid. Yet past payments were dividends; they did not extinguish that investment under the agreements. Giving up those rights without equivalent compensation would surrender taxpayer value, regardless of whether Washington writes another check.

His more recent relisting proposal emphasizes the estimated value of Treasury’s retained common shares. If Treasury sells only a small portion, most of that headline valuation would remain an unsold asset—not cash received. Unsold shares have economic value, but that value must be compared with the rights and future income taxpayers surrender, together with the cost of continuing federal support. Merely replacing a valuable senior claim with an estimated common-stock value does not establish a gain.

Any eventual stock sales must pass the same test. Selling an income-producing asset generates cash while relinquishing future income. Neither the sale proceeds nor the value of the remaining shares can simply be presented as wealth newly created by privatization.

A significant part of the shares’ value would reflect continuing federal support and privileges unavailable on equivalent terms to competing mortgage guarantors (a privilege that may violate the Equal Protection Clause of the U.S. Constitution). To the extent an underpriced government backstop increases share prices, Washington would be helping support that valuation at taxpayers’ expense. That subsidy cannot simply be counted as a taxpayer windfall.

Before conservatorship, Fannie and Freddie’s securities expressly disclaimed a federal guarantee. Investors nevertheless assumed Washington would prevent a default. That was the “implicit guarantee.”

Ackman wants eventual release with explicit contractual Treasury backing. His January 2025 exit plan assumed roughly $445 billion would become available for future support, including about $191 billion already drawn. Trump cannot create authority for those commitments merely by signing an executive order. Anything beyond existing statutory authority requires congressional approval, which a Democratic-controlled Congress will likely refuse to grant.

While private investors would absorb initial losses, taxpayers would remain exposed to catastrophic losses. Meanwhile, surrendering Treasury’s senior rights would allow more earnings to flow to private shareholders. Ackman’s plan entrenches the moral hazard that contributed to the original collapse and bailout. Global Hedge Funds Suffered One of Their Largest Declines Since COVID on Thursday

Bloomberg
10/23/2026 
Global hedge funds suffered one of their broadest declines since the Covid pandemic following the stock market selloff on Thursday, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc.’s prime brokerage desk.

“For the first time since Covid, all three broad equity strategies fell more than 1% on the same day,” the firm said in a note to clients. 

Global fundamental long/short managers were down 1.4% at the market close on Thursday, their worst day since July 16, with telecommunications, media and technology-focused funds falling by an average of 2.7%, according to the note. Global systematic long/short managers were hit by their third-worst day since December 2023, dropping 1.3%. 
Even multistrategy platforms — the pod shops whose broad mix of portfolio managers are designed to protect against firm-wide drawdowns — slid 1.9% for their second-worst day since the April 2025 tariff selloff.

Tech stocks in the US were sold heavily on Thursday on mounting concerns over whether massive spending on artificial intelligence will bear fruit. The Nasdaq 100 Index slid 2.9%, the most since June, as fears over oil-induced inflation added to the woes. Even bearish positions aren’t necessarily paying off during a volatile earnings season. 

“Based on estimates from our prime book, more than two-thirds of hedge funds finished down on the day as concentrated shorts were squeezed further in the second half of the session,” the prime brokerage said.

Asia fundamental long/short managers also lost money, with month-to-date declines at 9.3%. Even so, their hedge fund returns remain broadly positive so far this year at 14.2%, according to the note.
The selloff was the latest chapter in a wild ride for AI stocks this year, as rallies in shares like SK Hynix Inc. and Micron Technology Inc.have been punctuated by painful declines. In July, a rout in technology shares pushed hedge fund Situational Awareness to the brink, raising fears that the AI bull run was losing steam.

J.P. Morgan has included bitcoin in the 2027 edition of its “Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions.”

I take this as a signal that J.P. Morgan does not expect bitcoin to disappear anytime soon.

More importantly, it is another sign that bitcoin is becoming a mature asset class within the investment universe.

Interestingly, J.P. Morgan excludes bitcoin from its main covariance matrices, which determine strategic asset allocations, citing instability and high volatility.

But when is a correlation truly stable? Stock and bond returns were negatively correlated for less than 30 years, roughly between 1990 and 2020. Before and after that period, correlations were positive.

After cash, gold and bitcoin have the lowest average correlations with other asset classes. And while high-yield bonds and equities are consistently treated as two distinct asset classes, their correlation tells a different story: they are very much alike.

Meanwhile, the correlation between bitcoin and gold is just 0.10, offering significant diversification benefits.

I think it is only a matter of time before scarce assets like bitcoin and gold, which protect against risks stocks and bonds don't cover, make their way into every long-term strategic asset allocation.

posts.text:
I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://github.com/ultrametricai/ultrametric

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup. 

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance. 

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot. 

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible). 

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time. 

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://ultrametric.ai/overall

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://ultrametric.ai/processes

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant. 

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on

The 10 Year Treasury Is Looking Beyond Inflation And Seeing Something Much Worse

The U.S. 10 year Treasury yield plunged roughly 18 basis points to 4.965%. The story is not just the size of the move. It is what rallied alongside bonds, what sold off, and where investors were buying.

The Signal Inside The Yield Curve

The strongest declines were in 5 and 7 year maturities, down about 19 basis points, versus 14 at 30 years and fewer than 5 at 3 months. Buying is concentrated in intermediate debt, suggesting a reassessment of future growth and monetary policy rather than simply imminent Fed cuts. The 30 year yield remains above 5.3%, showing that long term fiscal and inflation risks have not disappeared.

Meanwhile Brent crude is above $112 and rising more than 3%. In a straightforward inflation scare, rising energy prices normally pressure yields higher. Instead Treasury yields are plunging. "If you're looking at the Sharpe ratio of a portfolio and you add Bitcoin, the numbers are astounding."
